title: What are things made of?

summary.text: A paper cup holds hot tea, yet paper goes soft in water. Everything around us is made of a material: wood, metal, plastic, glass, fabric or paper, and a few more. Your child hunts for each material at home, and learns to tell them apart by looking, touching, tapping and lifting. Then they test a paper cup against a newspaper cone, and cut the cup open. They find a thin plastic skin inside. Many things are made of more than one material.
summary.art: A girl kneeling on a kitchen floor beside six heaps of things: a wooden belan, a steel tumbler, a plastic box, a glass jar, a folded cotton towel and a paper bag.

intro.hook: Tea from a paper cup does not leak. But paper goes soft and soggy in water. So how can a paper cup hold tea?
intro.text: Look around the room. The door, the fan, the bucket, the window, your shirt and your book are all made of something. What a thing is made of is called its material. In this unit you learn six materials: wood, metal, plastic, glass, fabric and paper. You find them all over your home. Then you solve the puzzle of the paper cup.
intro.art: A woman holding a small white paper cup of tea, and a curious girl beside her pointing at the cup with a puzzled face.

outcomes: By the end I can name six materials (wood, metal, plastic, glass, fabric and paper) and find things made of each one at home.
By the end I can tell what a thing is made of by looking at it, touching it, tapping it and lifting it.
By the end I can say that one material can make many things, and one thing can be made of more than one material.
By the end I can say where wood, paper, cotton cloth, metal, glass and plastic come from.
By the end I can make a guess, test it, and say what I saw in the Paper Cup Puzzle.

terms.meaning: A material is what a thing is made of.
terms.example: A spoon can be made of the material steel, or wood, or plastic.
terms.art: Three spoons in a row: a shiny steel spoon, a brown wooden spoon and a red plastic spoon.

terms.meaning: Wood comes from trees. It is hard, and it has thin lines in it called the grain.
terms.example: A wooden chopping board, a door and a pencil are made of wood.
terms.art: A close look at a wooden chopping board showing brown grain lines, with a pencil lying on it.

terms.meaning: Metal is hard and often shiny. Steel, iron, aluminium, copper and gold are metals. A metal thing rings when you tap it.
terms.example: A steel tumbler, a key and a coin are made of metal.
terms.art: A shiny steel tumbler, a key and a one-rupee coin, with small lines around the tumbler to show it ringing.

terms.meaning: Plastic is a material made in factories, mostly from oil. It is light, and it can be made in any colour and shape.
terms.example: A bucket, a mug and a lunch box are often made of plastic.
terms.art: A bright blue plastic bucket with a red plastic mug inside, and a green plastic lunch box beside them.

terms.meaning: Glass is hard and smooth, and you can usually see through it. It is made by melting sand in a very hot fire. Glass can break into sharp pieces.
terms.example: A window, a jar and a mirror are made of glass.
terms.art: A glass jar of pickle on a sunny windowsill, with light shining through the window glass.

terms.meaning: Fabric is another word for cloth. It is soft and bends easily. It is made of many thin threads woven together.
terms.example: A saree, a shirt and a towel are made of fabric.
terms.art: A folded cotton saree and a towel, with a close-up circle showing tiny threads crossing over and under each other.

terms.meaning: Paper is a thin sheet made of tiny plant threads pressed together. It tears easily and goes soft when it gets wet.
terms.example: A book, a newspaper and a paper bag are made of paper.
terms.art: A newspaper, a notebook and a brown paper bag, with one sheet torn to show a fuzzy edge.

explanations.concept: Everything is made of a material
explanations.definition: A material is what a thing is made of. Wood, metal, plastic, glass, fabric and paper are six materials.
explanations.description: Every thing you can touch is made of a material. A chair might be made of wood. A tumbler might be made of steel, which is a metal. There are more materials than these six. Clay, stone, rubber and leather are materials too. Even you are made of materials, like bone, skin and hair.
examples: In the kitchen: a steel kadai, a glass jar, a plastic dabba, a wooden ladle, a cotton towel and a paper bag.
A clay diya for Karthigai Deepam is made of clay, another material.
Your rubber chappal is made of rubber.
explanations.context: This card says what a material is. In the Material Hunt, you sorted kitchen things by material.
explanations.art: A kitchen shelf with a steel kadai, a glass jar, a plastic dabba, a wooden ladle, a folded towel and a paper bag, each with a small label.

explanations.concept: How to tell what a thing is made of
explanations.definition: You can often tell a thing's material by looking at it, touching it, tapping it and lifting it.
explanations.description: Wood has thin lines called grain, and it sounds dull when you knock on it. Metal is hard and often shiny. It feels cold to touch, and it rings when you tap it. Plastic is light and smooth, and it can be any colour. Glass is hard and smooth, and you can usually see through it. Fabric is soft and bends, and you can see its threads up close. Paper is thin, tears easily and goes soggy in water.
examples: Tap a steel plate with a spoon: ting! Tap a wooden board: tok.
Lift a steel tiffin and a plastic tiffin of the same size. The steel one is heavier.
Hold a cotton towel up to the light. You can see tiny holes between the threads.
explanations.context: This card shows how to be a material detective, using your eyes, hands and ears.
explanations.art: A boy tapping a steel plate with a spoon and listening, while a girl beside him looks at the grain on a wooden board.

explanations.concept: One material makes many things, and one thing can have many materials
explanations.definition: One material, like steel, can be made into many different things. And one thing, like a pencil, can be made of more than one material.
explanations.description: Steel makes tumblers, spoons, plates, keys and train carriages. Paper makes books, tickets and bags. A thing gets its name from its shape and its job, not from its material. Many things are made of two or more materials. Each material does one part of the job. A paper cup is paper outside, so it stays stiff. Inside it has a thin skin of plastic, so the water stays in.
examples: A pencil is wood outside, with a grey stick inside called graphite. Many pencils also have paint and a rubber on the end.
An umbrella has a fabric top, metal spokes and a plastic or wooden handle.
A spoon can be steel, wood, plastic or even silver, and it is still a spoon.
explanations.context: In the Paper Cup Puzzle, you cut a paper cup open and found a thin plastic skin inside. This card explains how one thing can be made of two materials.
explanations.art: A paper cup cut open and laid flat, with a thin clear plastic skin peeling away from the inside, next to an open umbrella with arrows to its fabric, metal and handle.

explanations.definition: Every material comes from something in nature: a plant, an animal, rock, sand or oil from under the ground.
explanations.description: Wood comes from trees. Paper is made from wood, or from other plant threads like old cotton rags, bamboo or sugarcane waste. Cotton cloth comes from the soft fluff that grows around the seeds of the cotton plant. Silk comes from the cocoons of silkworms, and wool from the coat of a sheep. Metal comes from rocks dug out of the ground. Glass is made from sand, melted in a very hot fire. Most plastic is made from oil or gas found deep under the ground.
examples: Karnataka makes more silk than any other state in India.
A paper mill in Tamil Nadu makes paper from bagasse, the dry stalks left after sugarcane juice is squeezed out.
Firozabad, a city in Uttar Pradesh, makes glass bangles from melted sand and other materials.
explanations.context: This card says where the six materials come from.
explanations.art: A simple chart with six arrows: a tree to a wooden chair, a cotton plant to a shirt, a rock to a steel spoon, sand to a glass jar, a dark oil drop to a plastic bucket, and a tree to a book.

agreed.text: Everything we can touch is made of one or more materials.
agreed.evidence: Every thing people have ever tested, from a spoon to a mountain, is made of materials that can be named and studied.

agreed.text: Many things are made of more than one material.
agreed.evidence: Cut open a paper cup and you find paper and plastic. Look at a pencil and you find wood, graphite and paint.

agreed.text: All materials come from nature in the end: from plants, animals, rocks, sand, or oil under the ground.
agreed.evidence: People can follow every material back to where it began. Wood comes from trees, steel from iron in rocks, and plastic mostly from oil.

challenging.claim: A thing is made of just one material, the one in its name.
challenging.who: Many of us, when we say 'a paper cup' or 'a steel almirah'
challenging.for: Names like 'paper cup' tell us the main material, and they are useful.
challenging.against: A paper cup has a thin plastic skin inside. A steel almirah has a glass mirror, a plastic handle and a metal lock. Most things are made of several materials.
challenging.context: This card is about the names we give things.

challenging.claim: Paper can only be made from trees.
challenging.who: Many people today, because most paper is made from wood
challenging.for: Most paper in shops is made from wood from trees.
challenging.against: Paper can be made from any plant threads. Long ago, paper was made from rags, bark and old fishing nets. Paper in India is also made from bamboo and from sugarcane waste.
challenging.context: This card is about what paper is made from.

challenging.who: Many people, because plastic does not rot like a banana peel
challenging.for: A plastic bag can stay in the ground or the sea for a very long time, maybe hundreds of years.
challenging.against: Sunlight slowly breaks plastic into tiny pieces. In 2016, scientists in Japan found bacteria that can slowly eat one kind of plastic, the kind used for water bottles.
challenging.context: This card is about how long plastic lasts.

big_questions.q: The paper cup is paper outside and plastic inside. Should we still call it a paper cup?
big_questions.hint: What does the name tell you? What does it leave out?

big_questions.q: If you could cut a steel spoon into smaller and smaller pieces, would every piece still be steel?
big_questions.hint: Scientists say yes, down to pieces far too small to see. The tiniest pieces are called atoms.

big_questions.q: Is there anything that is not made of a material? What about light, a shadow or a song?
big_questions.hint: Can you touch it? Can you put it in a box?

big_questions.q: Your wooden chair was once part of a living tree. Is there still a little tree in the chair?
big_questions.hint: Look at the grain. Those lines show how the tree grew, year by year.

story.title: The Game on the Train
story.note: Madurai is a city in Tamil Nadu. Paati means grandmother in Tamil. Kavya, Arjun and Paati are made up.
text: Kavya was six. One morning she sat by a train window with her cousin Arjun and their grandmother, Paati. They were going from Chennai to Madurai, to visit their aunt.
Arjun was five. He could not sit still. After ten minutes he said, 'Paati, I'm bored. When will we get there?'
'Not till the evening,' said Paati. 'So let's play my game. It is called What Is It Made Of?'
'How do you play?' asked Kavya.
'I point at a thing,' said Paati. 'You tell me its material. A material is what a thing is made of.'
Paati tapped the window. Tak, tak.
'Glass!' said Kavya. 'I can see the fields through it.'
'Yes,' said Paati. 'Glass is made from sand, melted in a fire hotter than any kitchen stove.'
Arjun grabbed his water bottle. It was cold and shiny. He tapped it with his fingernail. Ting!
'Metal!' he shouted.
'Steel,' said Paati. 'Steel is a metal. Metal rings when you tap it.'
Kavya stroked the end of Paati's saree. It was soft, and when she looked close, she saw tiny threads going over and under each other.
'Fabric,' said Kavya. 'Cloth.'
'Cotton cloth,' said Paati. 'Cotton grows on a plant, as soft white fluff around the seeds.'
Then Kavya opened her lunch box. It was blue and very light. She tapped the lid. Tock.
'Plastic,' she said. Paati nodded.
Paati's walking stick leaned against the seat. Arjun ran his finger down it. It had thin brown lines from top to bottom.
'Wood,' said Paati. 'Those lines are called the grain. They show how the tree grew.'
'And your newspaper is paper,' said Kavya. 'That's six!'
Then Paati held up Kavya's pencil. 'And this?'
'Wood,' said Arjun at once.
Kavya took the pencil and looked at the sharp end. 'Not all wood,' she said. 'The point is grey. Wood is brown.'
'You are both right,' said Paati. 'The outside is wood. The grey stick in the middle is called graphite. It is a soft grey material that comes out of the ground.'
'So a pencil is two materials,' said Kavya.
Arjun counted on his fingers. 'Wood, the grey stick, the yellow paint, and the pink rubber at the top. Four!'
'Many things are made of more than one material,' said Paati. 'A good detective looks at every part.'
Just then a woman came down the coach with a big steel can. 'Coffee, coffee! Chai, chai!' she called.
Paati bought a coffee. It came in a small white paper cup. Steam curled up from the top.
Arjun stared at the cup. 'Paati, paper goes soggy in water. I spilled water on my drawing once, and it tore. Why is your cup not leaking?'
'That is a very good question,' said Paati. 'What do you think?'
'Magic paper,' said Arjun.
'Maybe the coffee is too quick to soak in,' said Kavya.
Paati smiled and sipped her coffee. 'Here is some homework for two detectives. When we get home, we will test a paper cup and find out.'

The train ran on past green paddy fields and tall palm trees. Kavya looked around the coach. The fan was metal. The switches were plastic. The ticket was paper. Paati's saree was cotton. Everything was made of something.
And some things, like her pencil, were made of more than one thing.
'Paati,' said Kavya, 'this whole train is part of your game.'
'The whole world is,' said Paati.
story.epiphany: Everything is made of a material, and many things are made of more than one. To name what a thing is made of, look at every part.
ask: What were the materials in Kavya's pencil?
Why do you think Paati's paper cup did not leak?
Look around you. Find one thing that is made of two materials.
art: A grandmother in a cotton saree sitting by a train window with two small children, the girl tapping the glass and the boy holding up a steel water bottle.
The girl looking closely at the grey point of a pencil while the boy counts on his fingers.
A woman coffee seller with a big steel can in a train coach, and the grandmother holding a small white paper cup while the boy stares at it.

games.title: Material Bingo: cover all six
games.players: 1 to 3 players and one caller. A grown-up can be the caller.
games.context: This is a board game. Each player has a board with six materials. The caller reads out a thing, and you put a bean on the material it is made of. The first to cover all six squares wins. With just a grown-up and a child, the grown-up calls and the child plays.

printables.title: 6 squares for each player's board
items: WOOD (draw a brown plank with lines)

items.f: A wooden belan for rolling chapatis
A lunch box, light and blue
A chopping board with brown lines
A pickle jar you can see through

items.b: Metal (with a plastic handle and a rubber ring)

items.f: A wooden spinning top, a pambaram

items.b: Paper, with thin sticks of bamboo

rules: Each player draws a board of six squares: wood, metal, plastic, glass, fabric and paper. Draw a small drawing in each square, so you can play without reading.
Each player has six beans or small stones.
The caller mixes the thing cards and reads one out loud.
Each player says what the thing is made of, then puts a bean on that square.
The caller reads the back of the card. A bean on the wrong square comes off. If the back names two materials, either one counts.
If a square already has a bean, wait for the next card.
If the cards run out before someone wins, mix them and use them again.
The first player to cover all six squares shouts 'Made of everything!' and wins. If two players finish on the same card, they both win.

setup.art: A sheet of paper divided into six squares, with a child's drawings of a plank, a tumbler, a bucket, a window, a shirt and a book.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a board with six materials.

setup.art: Two children with bingo boards and a small heap of rajma beans each, while a woman reads a card that says 'A key'.
setup.caption: 2. Hear the thing. Put a bean on the right material.

flow.do: 1. Help each player fold a sheet into six squares. 2. Your child draws one material in each square. 3. Give each player six beans.
flow.say: Draw a board with six squares. In each square, draw one material: wood, metal, plastic, glass, fabric and paper.
flow.kid: Fold your paper into six squares. Draw one material in each square.
flow.parent: A child who cannot write yet can draw: a brown plank for wood, a tumbler for metal, a bucket for plastic, a window for glass, a shirt for fabric and a book for paper.

flow.do: 1. Mix the thing cards. 2. Read one card at a time. 3. Each player puts a bean on a square. 4. Read the back.
flow.say: A key. What is a key made of? Put your bean on that square.
flow.kid: Listen to the card. What is the thing made of? Put a bean on that square.

ask.q: How do you know a key is metal?
good: It rings when you drop it.

flow.parent: Some things are made of more than one material, like a pressure cooker with a plastic handle. Accept any answer that matches the back of the card. If your child says something else that could be true, ask 'How could we check?'

flow.do: Ask the check question. Then play again with a new caller.
flow.say: A pressure cooker. Is it made of only one material?
flow.kid: Is a pressure cooker made of only one material?

check.q: What is a pressure cooker made of?
options: Metal, with a plastic handle and a rubber ring
check.why: The pot is metal, so it can go on the fire. The handle is plastic, so it stays cool enough to hold. The rubber ring keeps the steam in.

games.title: Bring Me Something Made Of...
games.players: 1 or more players and one caller.
games.context: This is a moving game. The caller names a material, and you race to find something in the room made of it, before the caller counts to 20.

items.b: Ideas: a pencil, a wooden spoon, a chair leg, a door
Ideas: a steel spoon, a key, a coin, a tumbler
Ideas: a comb, a bucket, a pen, a toy
Point to it, do not carry it. Ideas: a window, a mirror, a jar
Ideas: a sock, a towel, a cushion cover, a dupatta
Ideas: a book, a newspaper, a paper bag, a calendar

rules: The caller picks a material card and reads it out.

The player finds something made of that material and brings it back before the caller counts to 20. With more than one player, everyone runs at once, and each player who brings back a right thing in time scores.
For glass, and for things too big to carry, like a door, the player does not carry anything. They run and touch it gently, and say what it is.
The player says how they know: what they saw, felt or heard.
One point for each right thing. Two points for a thing made of two materials, if the player names both.
The game ends when each material card has been called once. The player with the most points wins. If you play alone, try to beat your own score next time.

setup.art: A woman holding up a card with the word WOOD and a drawing of a plank, counting on her fingers.
setup.caption: 1. The caller reads a material and starts counting.

setup.art: A girl running back across a living room holding up a wooden spoon, while a boy stands by a window touching the glass with one finger.
setup.caption: 2. Bring it back, or touch it if it is glass.

flow.do: 1. Clear the floor of toys. 2. Show your child the six material cards. 3. Tell them the glass rule: touch glass gently, do not carry it.
flow.say: I will call a material. You find something made of it before I count to 20. For glass, don't carry it. Just touch it gently and tell me.
flow.kid: Listen for the material. Find something made of it. For glass, just touch it.
flow.parent: Glass can break into sharp pieces, so glass things stay where they are.

flow.do: 1. Read a card. 2. Count to 20 out loud. 3. When your child comes back, ask how they know.
flow.say: Metal! One, two, three... What did you bring? How do you know it is metal?
flow.kid: Find something made of metal. Bring it back. Say how you know.

ask.q: How do you know it is metal?
good: It rings when I tap it.
It is heavy for its size.

flow.parent: The reason matters more than the speed. Praise a child who taps or lifts the thing to check.

flow.do: Play one last round with a new rule. Your child must find a thing made of two materials.
flow.say: Last round. Find one thing made of two materials, and tell me both.
flow.kid: Find one thing made of two materials. Name them both.

check.q: Which of these is made of two materials?
options: A knife with a plastic handle
check.why: The blade is steel and the handle is plastic. A cotton sock is only fabric, and a steel spoon is only metal.

experiments.title: The Paper Cup Puzzle: is it only paper?
experiments.context: In this experiment you pour water into a paper cup and into a cone made of newspaper. You watch what happens to each. Then a grown-up cuts the paper cup open, and you look inside.
experiments.question: Paper goes soggy in water. So why does a paper cup hold water? Is a paper cup made only of paper?
experiments.predict: Guess first. When we pour water into the newspaper cone, what will happen? What will happen in the paper cup? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both cups get the same amount of water, three spoonfuls each. Both are held over the same steel plate, and we watch both for the same time. Only the cup is different.

materials.item: a paper cup, the kind used for tea or water (ask a tea stall for a clean used one, or buy a pack at any small shop)
half a sheet of newspaper
sticky tape or a stapler
a steel plate
a tumbler of water and a spoon
scissors, for the grown-up
paper and crayons for the results

experiments.safety: Only a grown-up uses the scissors.

schedule.what: Guess, pour water into a newspaper cone and a paper cup, watch both, then cut the paper cup open and look inside.

experiments.record: Draw the two cups side by side. Draw what the water did in each one. Then draw the inside of the cut-open paper cup, and colour the plastic skin a different colour from the paper.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: Went dark and soft. Water dripped onto the plate in about a minute.
Stayed in the cup. The outside stayed dry.
Paper outside, a thin plastic skin inside

setup.art: A woman's hands rolling half a sheet of newspaper into an ice-cream cone shape and taping the side, with a white paper cup beside it on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Roll newspaper into a cone. Put a paper cup next to it.

setup.art: A girl holding the newspaper cone and the paper cup over a steel plate while her mother spoons water into each.
setup.caption: 2. Pour three spoons of water into each, over a plate.

setup.art: The newspaper cone dark and dripping onto the plate, and the paper cup dry and full.
setup.caption: 3. Watch. What happens to each?

setup.art: A paper cup cut down one side and opened flat, with a thin clear skin peeling from the inside at a torn edge.
setup.caption: 4. A grown-up cuts the cup open. Look inside.

flow.do: 1. Put the paper cup and half a sheet of newspaper on the table. 2. Let your child hold and feel both.
flow.say: Here is a paper cup and some newspaper. What is the cup made of? What is the newspaper made of?
flow.kid: Feel the paper cup. Feel the newspaper. What are they made of?

ask.q: What is the cup made of?
good: It says paper cup, so paper.

flow.parent: Most children say paper. That is the right first guess. Don't say yet that there is anything else.

flow.do: 1. Roll the newspaper into a cone, about as big as the cup. 2. Tape or staple the side. 3. Fold the tip up so it is closed.
flow.say: Let's make a newspaper cup too. Now we have two paper cups.
flow.kid: Watch the grown-up make a cup out of newspaper.
flow.parent: The cone does not need to be neat. It only has to hold water for a few seconds.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess what will happen in each cup. Write or draw their guesses.
flow.say: We will pour water into both. What will happen to the newspaper cup? What will happen to the paper cup? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. What will the water do in each cup? Why?

good: Paper gets wet, so both will leak.
The paper cup will hold it, because people drink tea from it.

flow.parent: Wait for a reason as well as a guess. Any guess is fine.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds both cups over the steel plate. 2. Spoon three spoonfuls of water into each. 3. Count slowly to 60 together. 4. Look at both cups and the plate.
flow.say: Hold them still over the plate. One spoon, two, three. Now let's count to 60 and watch.
flow.kid: Hold both cups over the plate. Count to 60. Watch the water.

good: The newspaper went dark and soft.
Water dripped out of the newspaper.
The paper cup is still full and dry outside.

flow.parent: The newspaper darkens almost at once, and usually drips within a minute. The paper cup stays dry outside. If the cone has not dripped yet, wait one more minute and squeeze it gently.

flow.do: Ask your child to explain what they saw.
flow.say: Both cups are paper. So why did only one leak? What could be different about the paper cup?
flow.kid: Both cups are paper. Why did only one leak?

flow.do: 1. Pour the water out of the paper cup. 2. Cut it down one side with scissors and open it flat. 3. Your child feels the inside and the outside. 4. Tear a strip slowly from the cut edge, and look at the torn edge.
flow.say: Feel the outside, then feel the inside. Are they the same? Now watch the edge as I tear it slowly.
flow.kid: Feel the outside of the cup. Feel the inside. Watch the edge when it tears.

good: The inside is smoother and shinier.
There is a thin clear skin.
The skin stretches when the paper tears.

flow.parent: The inside of most paper cups has a very thin skin of plastic. When you tear slowly, the paper tears first, and the clear skin stretches before it breaks. If you can't see it, soak the strip in water for five minutes. Then rub the paper side with a thumbnail. The soft paper rubs off, and the clear skin is left.

flow.do: 1. Say together what you found. 2. Your child draws the results. 3. Ask the check question.
flow.say: So what is a paper cup made of? How do you know?
flow.kid: What is a paper cup made of? How do you know?

ask.q: What is a paper cup made of?
good: Paper outside and a plastic skin inside.
The plastic keeps the water in, and the paper makes it stiff.

check.q: Why did the paper cup hold water, when the newspaper cone leaked?
options: The paper cup has a thin plastic skin inside
The paper cup was made of thicker newspaper
The water was colder in the paper cup
check.why: Paper soaks up water, like the newspaper did. The paper cup has a thin skin of plastic on the inside, and water cannot soak through plastic. So the cup is made of two materials.

activities.title: The Material Hunt: which material is used most in our kitchen?
activities.context: In this activity you hunt for things in the kitchen and sort them by material. You guess first which material you will find the most of, then you count.

materials.item: 6 sheets of paper, each with one material drawn and written on it: wood, metal, plastic, glass, fabric, paper
a pencil for tally marks

activities.safety: Glass things stay on the shelf. Only point to them, and a grown-up makes the tally mark.

schedule.what: Guess which material there is most of, hunt the kitchen, make tally marks, and count.

activities.record: Under each material card, make one tally mark for each thing you found. Circle the material with the most marks.

setup.art: Six sheets of paper on a kitchen floor, each with a drawing: a plank, a tumbler, a bucket, a window, a shirt and a book.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the six material cards.

setup.art: A boy putting a steel ladle on the metal card, while his grandmother points at a glass jar on a shelf and makes a tally mark on the glass card.
setup.caption: 2. Find things. Put them on the right card, or make a mark.

flow.do: 1. Lay the six material cards on the kitchen floor. 2. Point to each one and name it.
flow.say: These are six materials. In our kitchen, which material do you think the most things are made of? Why?
flow.kid: Look at the six cards. Which material is used most in our kitchen? Guess, and say why.

good: Metal, because we have lots of steel plates.
Plastic, because of all the dabbas.

flow.do: 1. Your child finds safe things and puts each one on its card. 2. For glass, they point, and you make a tally mark. 3. For big things like the fridge, they make a tally mark.
flow.say: Find a thing. What is it made of? How do you know? Put it on that card.
flow.kid: Find a thing. Say what it is made of. Put it on the card.

ask.q: How do you know this is plastic?
good: It went tock when I tapped it.

flow.parent: Let your child tap, lift and look. If they are not sure, ask 'Is it shiny? Does it ring? Can you see through it?' A thing with two materials, like a knife with a plastic handle, goes between two cards.

flow.do: 1. Count the things or marks on each card together. 2. Compare with the guess. 3. Put everything back.
flow.say: Let's count. Which card has the most? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Count the things on each card. Which has the most?

good: My guess was wrong. It was plastic.

flow.parent: In many Indian kitchens, metal wins because of steel plates and vessels. In others, plastic wins. Either result is a real finding.

activities.title: Rubbing Rainbow: what does each material's surface show?
activities.context: In this activity you put thin paper over different materials and rub with a crayon. Each material leaves its own pattern, or none at all.

materials.item: thin paper, like printer paper or the back of an old calendar
wax crayons, with the paper wrapper peeled off one
a jute bag, a woven mat or a coarse cotton cloth
a jute bag, a towel or a woven mat
a steel plate
a plastic basket or a plastic comb

activities.record: Stick the rubbings on one page. Under each one, write or draw the material it came from.

setup.art: A sheet of paper laid over a wooden chopping board, and a child rubbing the side of a crayon across it.
setup.caption: 1. Lay paper on the material. Rub with the side of a crayon.

setup.art: Four rubbings side by side: wavy wood grain lines, a criss-cross jute pattern, a blank smooth patch for steel, and a pattern of holes from a plastic basket.
setup.caption: 2. Compare the patterns.

flow.do: 1. Lay the paper over the wooden board. 2. Show your child how to rub with the flat side of a crayon.
flow.say: Rub gently with the side of the crayon. Watch what comes up.
flow.kid: Rub the side of the crayon over the paper. What do you see?
flow.parent: These lines are the grain of the wood. They show how the tree grew. A painted or polished table may show nothing, so use an unpainted board.

flow.do: Make a rubbing of the jute bag or towel, the steel plate and the plastic basket, each on new paper.
flow.say: Before you rub, guess. Will the steel plate make a pattern? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first: will the steel plate make a pattern? Then rub the cloth, the plate and the basket.

ask.q: What did the steel plate make?
good: It is too smooth to make a pattern.

flow.parent: Jute and coarse woven cloth show criss-cross threads. A towel shows soft bumps. Steel is so smooth that the rubbing is plain colour.

flow.do: Mix up the rubbings. Ask your child to say which material made each one.
flow.say: Can you tell which material made each rubbing, just by looking?
flow.kid: Which material made each pattern?

check.q: A rubbing shows tiny lines going over and under each other. What made it?
check.why: Fabric is made of threads woven over and under each other. Steel and glass are smooth, so they leave no pattern.

activities.title: Look Closer: the threads in paper and cloth
activities.context: In this activity you tear paper and pull a thread from cloth, and look closely at the edges. You find that both are made of thin threads.

materials.item: a sheet of newspaper or a paper napkin
an old cotton cloth with a frayed edge, like an old handkerchief or a torn duster
a magnifying glass, if you have one

activities.record: Draw the torn edge of the paper and one thread from the cloth, as big as you can.

setup.art: A child tearing a strip of newspaper slowly and holding the torn edge up to a window.
setup.caption: 1. Tear paper slowly. Hold the edge up to the light.

setup.art: A child pulling one thread out from the frayed edge of an old cotton cloth.
setup.caption: 2. Pull one thread out of an old cloth.

flow.do: 1. Your child tears the paper slowly. 2. Hold the torn edge up to a window or a lamp.
flow.say: Look at the torn edge against the light. What do you see?
flow.kid: Tear the paper slowly. Hold the edge up to the light. What do you see?
flow.parent: The fuzzy hairs are plant threads, called fibres. Paper is made of millions of them pressed together.

flow.do: 1. Find a frayed edge on the old cloth. 2. Help your child pull out one thread. 3. Look at the hole and the thread.
flow.say: Pull one thread out. Look where it came from. What is the cloth made of?
flow.kid: Pull one thread out. What is the cloth made of?

ask.q: What is the cloth made of?
good: Lots of threads going over and under.

flow.parent: Cotton cloth is woven from cotton threads, and each thread is twisted from even thinner cotton fibres.

flow.do: Ask your child how paper and cloth are alike.
flow.say: How are paper and cloth the same? How are they different?
flow.kid: How are paper and cloth the same?

good: Cloth threads are woven, and paper threads are squashed together.

activities.title: Foil or Not? The Scrunch Ball test
activities.context: In this activity you scrunch kitchen foil and an empty chips packet into balls, and watch what each one does. Both are shiny inside. Are they the same material?

materials.item: a piece of kitchen foil, about the size of your hand (or the foil back of an empty medicine strip)
an empty chips or biscuit packet that is shiny inside, wiped clean

activities.record: Draw the two balls after one minute. Write or draw what each one is made of.

setup.art: A child's two hands, one holding a piece of kitchen foil and the other an empty shiny chips packet.
setup.caption: 1. Look at both. Both are shiny.

setup.art: On a table, a tight foil ball and a chips packet ball that has opened up loosely.
setup.caption: 2. Scrunch both into balls. Put them down and watch.

flow.do: Show your child the foil and the inside of the chips packet.
flow.say: Both of these are shiny. Kitchen foil is a metal called aluminium. Is the chips packet metal too? What do you think, and why?
flow.kid: The foil and the chips packet are both shiny. Is the chips packet metal too? Why do you think so?

flow.do: 1. Your child scrunches each one into a tight ball. 2. Put both balls on the table. 3. Watch for one minute.
flow.say: Squeeze each one into a tight ball. Put them down. Now watch them for a minute.
flow.kid: Scrunch the foil and the chips packet into balls. Put them down. Watch them for a minute.

good: The chips packet opened up again.

flow.parent: Kitchen foil stays scrunched, like most metal sheets. Most chips packets slowly open up, because they are mostly plastic. If your packet stays scrunched, it may have a real foil layer inside. That is a good find too.

flow.do: Tell your child what the chips packet is made of. Ask the check question.
flow.say: A chips packet is mostly plastic. On the inside it has a very, very thin coat of metal, to keep air and light away from the chips.
flow.kid: A chips packet is mostly plastic, with a thin metal coat inside.

check.q: The chips packet opened up again after scrunching. What does that tell you?
options: It is mostly plastic, not metal like the foil
check.why: The foil stayed scrunched, as metal sheets do. The packet sprang back, as plastic does. It looks like metal only because of a very thin metal coat.

projects.title: A Shoebox Room: one material for each part
projects.context: In this project you make a little room inside a shoebox or a carton. You use a different material for each part, and label them all.

materials.item: a shoebox or a small carton
ice-cream sticks or a few dry twigs, for wood
a clean bottle cap or kitchen foil, for metal
a piece of clear plastic from old packaging, for a window
a scrap of cloth
paper, glue, crayons and sticky tape

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the window hole.

schedule.what: Plan the room. Cut a window and fit the clear plastic. Make a bed or a table from ice-cream sticks.
Add a cloth bedsheet or curtain, a foil mirror or a bottle-cap plate, and paper pictures for the walls. Label every material and show the room to the family.

projects.record: The finished room, with a small paper label on each part naming its material.

setup.art: A shoebox on its side with a window hole cut in the back, covered with clear plastic.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a window and cover it with clear plastic.

setup.art: The finished shoebox room with an ice-cream stick bed, a cloth sheet, a foil mirror, a bottle-cap plate and small paper labels.
setup.caption: 2. Add parts made of each material, and label them.

flow.do: 1. Lay out all the materials. 2. Ask your child what each part of the room could be made of.
flow.say: We are making a little room. What could the bed be made of? The window? The curtain?
flow.kid: Plan your room. What will each part be made of?

ask.q: Why is a real window made of glass?

flow.do: 1. Cut a window hole in the box and tape clear plastic over it. 2. Your child glues ice-cream sticks into a bed or a table.
flow.say: Real windows are glass. Our window is clear plastic, because glass can break and cut. Now build the bed from wood.
flow.kid: Glue the sticks into a bed. The window is plastic, so it is safe.
flow.parent: Talk about why the model uses plastic for the window. It is see-through like glass, but it does not break into sharp pieces.

flow.do: On day 2, your child adds a cloth sheet, a foil mirror or a bottle-cap plate, and paper pictures.
flow.say: Now add fabric, metal and paper. Which part will be fabric?
flow.kid: Add a cloth sheet, a foil mirror and paper pictures.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a label for each part, and a grown-up writes the word on it. 2. They show the room and name every material.
flow.say: Show us your room. Tell us what each part is made of.
flow.kid: Show your room. Name every material.

check.q: Why did we use clear plastic for the window in the model?
options: It is see-through like glass, and safer
check.why: Clear plastic lets light through, like glass, but it bends instead of breaking into sharp pieces.

challenges.title: Make a Hand Fan That Works
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. It is a hot afternoon and the power is off. You make a hand fan, and test which material works best.
challenges.problem: The power has gone and the fan has stopped. You need a hand fan. Which material makes the best one: paper, cloth or plastic?
constraints: The fan must be light enough to wave for one minute.
It must move enough air to lift a small strip of paper from a hand-length away.
materials: a handkerchief or a scrap of cloth
an old plastic folder or a piece of a plastic bag
a small strip of paper to test with
a piece of cardboard from an old box
general: Fold a sheet of paper back and forth like a zigzag, then pinch one end. This is a folding fan.
Tape a flat piece of cardboard to a stick, like a small bat.
In South India, many families once used fans made of dried palm leaves.
creative: Stiffen the cloth by taping ice-cream sticks across it.
Fold the plastic folder into a zigzag. It springs back, so it moves air with each wave.
Make one fan from two materials: a paper fan with a stick handle.
challenges.your_turn: Make one fan from each material, all about the same size. Wave each one ten times at the paper strip from the same distance. Which one lifts the strip best? Draw your best fan and label its materials.

setup.art: Three home-made fans on a table: a zigzag paper fan, a floppy handkerchief taped to a stick, and a zigzag plastic folder fan.
setup.caption: 1. Make a fan from paper, cloth and plastic.

setup.art: A girl waving a zigzag paper fan at a thin strip of paper on the edge of a table, the strip lifting up.
setup.caption: 2. Test each fan on a paper strip.

flow.do: Read the problem to your child. Show the paper, cloth and plastic.
flow.say: The power is off and it is hot. Which material would make the best fan? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: It is hot. Which material makes the best fan? Why?

good: Paper, because it is light and you can fold it.

flow.do: 1. Help your child make one fan from each material, all about the same size. 2. Show the zigzag fold for the paper.
flow.say: Fold the paper forward, then back, then forward. Pinch one end. That is your fan.
flow.kid: Make one fan from paper, one from cloth and one from plastic. Fold the paper back and forth.

flow.do: 1. Put a paper strip on the table, with half of it hanging over the edge and a book on the other half. 2. Your child waves each fan ten times from one hand-length away.
flow.say: Wave each fan ten times from the same place. Which one lifts the strip best?
flow.kid: Wave each fan ten times at the strip. Which works best?

good: The cloth one was too floppy.
The plastic one worked well too.

flow.parent: A stiff fan pushes the most air. Floppy cloth or a thin plastic bag bends away. Whichever fan wins is a real result, so write it down.

flow.do: Ask the check question.
flow.say: If the cloth fan pushed little air, why do you think that was?
flow.kid: Why did the floppy fan push so little air?

check.q: A floppy fan, like one made of cloth, pushes very little air. Why?
options: Cloth is soft and bends too easily
Cloth is too heavy to lift
check.why: Fabric is soft and floppy, so it bends away instead of pushing the air. A stiffer fan pushes the air along.

items.p: Here is a kitchen shelf. Say or write the material of each thing.
items.why: Each clue tells you the material. Shiny and grey is metal. See-through is glass. Light and bright is plastic. Brown lines are wood grain. Soft is fabric. Thin and easy to tear is paper.
items.art: A kitchen shelf with a steel tumbler, a glass jar, a blue plastic lunch box, a wooden ladle, a folded towel and a brown paper bag, each with an empty label.

items.p: Draw a line from each thing to the material it is usually made of.
items.why: Most chairs are wood, windows are glass, buckets are plastic, sarees are fabric, books are paper and keys are metal. Some of these can be made of other materials too.
items.art: A chair, a window, a bucket, a saree, a book and a key on the left, and six material words on the right, mixed up.

items.p: Colour the metal things yellow and the wooden things brown.
items.why: Metal things are hard and shiny, and ring when tapped. Wooden things have grain lines and sound dull when knocked.

items.p: Draw something in your home that is made of glass. Draw a ring around the glass part.
items.a: A drawing of a window, a mirror, a jar or a bottle, with a ring around the glass.
items.why: A strong drawing rings only the glass part. A window has glass in a wooden or metal frame, so only the middle is glass.
items.art: A blank box with a small drawing of a house wall at the top.

items.p: You tap a tumbler with a spoon. It rings: ting! It is shiny and cold. What is the tumbler made of?
items.why: Metal is shiny, feels cold to touch and rings when you tap it. A plastic tumbler would go tock, and a paper one would make almost no sound.

items.p: Three of these are made of fabric. Which one is not?
items.why: A towel, a shirt and a dupatta are fabric, soft cloth made of threads. A spoon is hard. It is usually metal, wood or plastic.

items.p: Remember the Paper Cup Puzzle, where water went into a newspaper cone and a paper cup. Why did the newspaper cone leak, while the paper cup held the water? Say it, and a grown-up writes it down.
items.a: The newspaper is only paper, and paper soaks up water. The paper cup has a thin plastic skin inside, and water cannot soak through it.
items.why: A strong answer says what was different: the plastic skin inside the paper cup.

items.p: Lakshmi and her brother Kiran are looking at a pencil.

views.says: A pencil is made of wood. Look, it is brown.
A pencil is made of many materials. The middle is grey, and there is paint and a rubber.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other one has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason. For Lakshmi: the grey middle is graphite, not wood, and the rubber is rubber. For Kiran: most of a pencil is wood, so he named the main material.
items.why: Both are partly right. Most of a pencil is wood, but a pencil is made of several materials. Looking at every part tells you the whole answer.

items.p: An umbrella has a fabric top, metal spokes and a plastic handle. How many different materials is it made of?
items.why: Fabric, metal and plastic make 3 materials. Each one does a job: the fabric keeps the rain off, the metal holds it open and the plastic handle is light to hold.
items.art: An open umbrella with arrows pointing to the fabric top, the thin metal spokes and the curved plastic handle.

items.p: Draw one thing at home that is made of two materials. Colour each material in a different colour.
items.a: For example, a knife with a steel blade and a plastic handle, coloured in two colours.
items.why: A strong drawing shows two clear parts, each made of a different material, and the child can name both.

items.p: Glass is made from sand.
items.why: True. Glass is made by melting sand with a few other materials in a very hot fire, then letting it cool.

items.p: You find a light, red, smooth box. You tap it: tock. You cannot see through it. What is it most likely made of?
items.why: Plastic is light and can be any colour, and it goes tock when tapped. Glass is usually see-through, and metal is heavier and rings.

items.p: Remember the Scrunch Ball test, where you scrunched kitchen foil and a chips packet. Your friend says a chips packet is metal, because it is shiny inside. What would you tell your friend? Use what you saw. Say it, and a grown-up writes it down.
items.a: The foil stayed scrunched, but the chips packet opened up again. So the packet is mostly plastic, with only a very thin metal coat inside.
items.why: A strong answer uses what the child saw: the two balls acted differently, so they are different materials.

items.p: Where does it come from? Sort these into 'From a plant' and 'From the ground'.
items.why: Cotton grows on a plant, and paper and wood come from trees. Steel comes from iron in rocks, glass from sand, and most plastic from oil. Iron, sand and oil are all dug or pumped out of the ground.

items.p: Draw the newspaper cone from the Paper Cup Puzzle, one minute after the water went in.
items.a: A dark, soft-looking cone with drops of water falling onto a plate.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the paper darker where it is wet, and water dripping out. Paper soaks up water and lets it through.

items.p: One material, like steel, can be made into many different things.
items.why: True. Steel makes tumblers, spoons, keys, plates and even train carriages. The shape and the job change, but the material is the same.

items.p: Three of these are usually made of plastic. Which one is not?
items.why: A bucket, a comb and a toothbrush handle are light and plastic. A steel tumbler is metal, and it rings when you tap it.

items.p: Why are windows made of glass and not wood? Say one good reason, and a grown-up writes it down.
items.a: Glass is see-through, so light comes in and we can see out. Wood would block the light.
items.why: A strong answer names what the glass does for the job. Glass also keeps out rain and wind while letting light in.

items.p: Why is a raincoat not made of paper?
opts: Paper goes soft and tears when it gets wet
Paper is too heavy to wear
items.why: Paper soaks up water, then goes soft and tears, like the newspaper cone in the Paper Cup Puzzle. A raincoat must keep water out, so it is made of plastic or a coated fabric.

items.p: Label the parts of a school water bottle with their materials: metal, plastic, rubber.
items.why: Each part has a job. The metal body is strong, the plastic lid is light, and the bendy rubber ring keeps the water in.
items.art: A school water bottle with a steel body, a blue plastic lid, and the lid turned over to show a black rubber ring.

items.p: Match each clue to the material.
pairs: It is shiny and rings when tapped
It tears easily and gets soggy in water
items.why: Each material has clues you can see, feel or hear. Detectives use these clues to name a material.

videos.title: How paper cups are made

videos.check: Found by search: "How Paper Cups Are Made" by How It's Made, 3 minutes 2 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.check: Found by search: "How was it made? Traditional Indian Weaving" by Victoria and Albert Museum, 3 minutes 8 seconds. A parent may preview it.

opts: What a thing is made of
quiz.why: A material is what a thing is made of, like wood, metal, plastic, glass, fabric or paper.

quiz.p: Which of these is made of fabric?
quiz.why: A cotton shirt is fabric, made of threads woven together. A steel plate is metal and a glass jar is glass.

quiz.p: You can see right through a window. What is it usually made of?
quiz.why: Glass is hard and see-through, so light comes in. Wood and paper block the light.

quiz.p: Which material has thin brown lines called grain?
quiz.why: The grain in wood shows how the tree grew. Glass and plastic have no grain.

quiz.p: Which of these is made of more than one material?
quiz.why: An umbrella has a fabric top, metal spokes and a handle. A sheet of paper is only paper, and a steel spoon is only metal.

quiz.p: Steel makes tumblers, spoons and keys. What does this show?
opts: One material can make many different things
Every material makes only one thing
Steel is a kind of plastic
quiz.why: One material can be shaped into many things. The name of a thing tells you its job, and the material tells you what it is made of.
Wood comes from trees. Glass is made from sand, and most plastic from oil.

quiz.p: Most plastic is made from what?
opts: Oil from deep under the ground
quiz.why: Most plastic is made in factories from oil or gas found deep under the ground. Glass is the material made from sand.

quiz.p: A paper cup holds water, but a cone made of newspaper leaks. What must the paper cup have on the inside?
quiz.why: A thin plastic skin lines the inside of most paper cups. Water cannot soak through plastic, so the cup holds water.

quiz.p: You pour water into a cone made of newspaper. What will happen?
opts: It goes dark and soft, and leaks
quiz.why: Paper soaks up water. The newspaper goes dark, then soft, and the water drips through.

applications: Builders choose the right material for each part of a house: concrete for walls, glass for windows and wood or metal for doors.
Kabadiwalas sort old things by material, so paper, metal and plastic can each be made into something new.
Doctors use steel for tools, because steel can be washed in very hot water and stays clean.
Tailors pick cotton for hot weather, because it lets air through and soaks up sweat.
Toy makers use soft fabric for toys for babies, because soft fabric has no sharp edges and does not hurt when it falls.

spotted.art: A kitchen shelf with a row of round steel tiffin boxes, stacked and shining.

spotted.art: A street stall with rods of colourful glass bangles, and a girl trying some on.

spotted.art: A man beside a hand cart with three neat piles: newspapers tied with string, metal tins and plastic bottles.

open_questions.q: How many different materials are there in the world?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists keep making new ones, and nobody has counted them all. Nobody knows how many more could be made.

open_questions.q: Can we make a plastic that rots away like a leaf, but is as strong as today's plastic?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists are trying. Some new plastics break down more easily, but none yet does every job as well as the old kind.

open_questions.q: How exactly do some bacteria eat plastic?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists found bacteria that slowly eat one kind of plastic. They are still finding out how they do it, and whether it could help clean up plastic waste.

ask_kids: What is your plate made of today?
Can you find something made of wood on the way to the shop?
What is your chappal made of?
If you could make a spoon out of any material, which would you choose? Why?
Which material would make a bad umbrella? Why?
Can you find a thing made of three materials?

jokes.j: Why did the newspaper go to the doctor?
What did the window say to the girl?
jokes.a: I can see right through you!

jokes.j: What kind of music do steel spoons like?
What has teeth but never bites?
What gets wetter the more it dries?
Why did the pencil stop writing?
What did the button say to the shirt?
What did the paper cup say to the tea?
jokes.a: Don't worry, I've got a plastic skin!

maths.problem: After a Material Hunt in the kitchen, the tally marks are: metal 7, plastic 5, glass 2. Which material had the most things?
maths.explain: 7 is more than 5, and 5 is more than 2. So metal had the most, and glass had the fewest.
maths.context: This is about the Material Hunt, where you sorted kitchen things by material and made tally marks.
maths.why_maths: Tally marks turn a heap of things into numbers we can compare at a glance.

maths.problem: In a Material Hunt, you find 6 things made of metal and 4 things made of plastic. How many more metal things did you find?
maths.explain: Line up the metal things and the plastic things in pairs. 4 pairs match, and 2 metal things are left over. 6 take away 4 is 2.
maths.context: This is about the Material Hunt, where you counted the things on each material card.
maths.why_maths: Taking away shows how much bigger one heap is than another.

maths.problem: A pencil has wood, a grey graphite middle, paint and a rubber at the end. How many materials is that?
maths.explain: Count one finger for each: wood, graphite, paint and rubber. That is 4.
maths.context: This is about the pencil from the story, The Game on the Train.
maths.why_maths: Counting the parts shows that even a small thing can be made of many materials.

warmup.q: What is a window usually made of?
Name one thing made of wood.
warmup.a: For example, a door, a chair, a pencil or a belan.

warmup.q: What sound does metal make when you tap it?

warmup.a: From the fluff around the seeds of the cotton plant.

warmup.q: What is inside a paper cup that keeps the water in?
What is most plastic made from?
warmup.a: Oil from deep under the ground.

founder: ideas/by_topic/materials-and-their-properties.md: the notebook's ideas on materials and sound (knock wood, metal and cloth) are used as tapping clues in the explanations and games, and its 'guessing game for hidden material' idea shaped Bring Me Something Made Of. Its transparency, heat and surface-tension activities belong to other units. The Class 3 unit on this subtopic uses paper making, salt from sea water, kitchen colours, milk plastic and the journey backwards, so this unit uses the paper cup test, a kitchen material hunt, crayon rubbings, torn-edge fibres and a scrunch test instead.
Cambridge Primary Science Stage 1, Unit 4.1 'What is it made of?': the materials hunt at home and naming the materials of everyday things.
science: Paper cups for hot and cold drinks are usually coated on the inside with a thin layer of polyethylene plastic, or sometimes another plastic, to keep the drink from soaking into the paper.
Most chips packets are made of plastic film with a very thin coating of aluminium on the inside, to keep out light and air.
Shosuke Yoshida and colleagues, 'A bacterium that degrades and assimilates poly(ethylene terephthalate)', Science 351 (2016): Ideonella sakaiensis, found in Japan, slowly breaks down PET plastic.

Fan Ye's Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu) records Cai Lun presenting paper to the emperor in 105 CE. Older paper fragments, including the Fangmatan map found in Gansu in 1986, show paper was made in China earlier.
Pencil 'lead' is graphite mixed with clay. It contains no lead.

roots.context: We have named the materials around us, and found that a paper cup is paper and plastic together. Now we ask what that tells us about things, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the Paper Cup Puzzle, the newspaper cone leaked, but the paper cup held its water. When the cup was cut open, you found a thin skin of plastic inside. The paper keeps the cup stiff, and the plastic keeps the water in. Many things are made of two or more materials, each doing its own part of the job.
deep_truth.habit: We name a thing after one material: a paper cup, a steel almirah, a wooden door. The name tells us only the main part. To know what a thing is made of, we have to look at every part.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Paper Cup Puzzle, the newspaper cone dripped within about a minute, while the paper cup stayed dry outside. When the cup was cut open, a thin clear skin stretched at the torn edge and could be peeled from the paper.

three.who_am_i: You are made of many materials too: bone, skin, hair, teeth and blood. Each one does its own job in your body.
three.what_is_life: Some materials are made by living beings. Trees make wood, cotton plants make cotton, and silkworms spin silk.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of things, and every one is made of materials. A few materials, used again and again, make most of what you see.

roots.thread: Steel makes a tumbler, a spoon and a train. A paper cup is paper and plastic together. All these materials come from the Earth: from trees, plants, rocks, sand and oil. Everything is conscious, including the tree that gave the wood and the rock that gave the steel. Many scientists disagree. They say only living beings, or only beings with brains, are aware.

teachings.teaching: The teacher Uddalaka tells his son Shvetaketu: when you know one lump of clay, you know everything made of clay. A pot, a cup and a lamp are only different names and shapes. The clay is what they really are.
teachings.link: In the Material Hunt, the metal card held a tumbler, a spoon and a plate. Their names were different, but they were all made of one material.

teachings.source: J.C. Bose, Response in the Living and Non-Living (1902)
teachings.teaching: The Indian scientist Jagadish Chandra Bose gave metal wires small electric shocks, again and again. He reported that their response grew weaker, then came back after a rest. He saw the same thing in plants and in muscles, and he called it fatigue, which means tiredness.
teachings.link: We usually sort the world into living beings and materials. Bose reported that a metal responds to what happens to it, much like a muscle does.

science.text: Every material is made of tiny particles called atoms, far too small to see. Wood, steel and plastic are made of different atoms, joined in different ways.
Scientists keep inventing new materials, and nobody knows how many different materials could be made.

other_view.view: Many scientists say Bose's metal wires changed because of changes on the metal's surface. For them, that is a chemical change. They say only living beings, or only beings with brains, are aware.

practice.title: Two spoons, eyes closed
practice.say: Close your eyes. I will put a spoon in each of your hands. One is steel and one is wood. Hold them still. Which one feels cooler? Now tap each one gently on the table, and listen. Which one rings? Open your eyes. Were you right? One spoon came from a rock and one from a tree.
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Hold one spoon in each hand. Which feels cooler? Tap each one. Which one rings? Now open your eyes.

ask: Which part of your body feels hard like wood, and which part feels soft like cloth?
If a thing is made of two materials, like a paper cup, which material is it really?
The scientist Jagadish Chandra Bose said a metal can get tired, like a muscle. What test could you try on a steel spoon?
roots.art: A girl with her eyes closed holding a steel spoon in one hand and a wooden spoon in the other, with a faint tree behind the wooden spoon and a faint rock behind the steel one.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, people said that paper was invented in China in the year 105, by a man named Cai Lun. He worked at the emperor's court. Old books say he made paper from tree bark, old cloth rags and worn-out fishing nets. He soaked and beat them into a mush, spread it thin on a screen, and let it dry. In the 1900s, archaeologists in China dug up pieces of paper that were older than Cai Lun. One piece, found at a place called Fangmatan in 1986, has a map drawn on it. Scientists still argue about its exact age, but most think it is more than 200 years older than Cai Lun. So Cai Lun did not invent paper. He made it better, and told the emperor about it. Paper reached India much later. Before that, people in South India wrote on dried palm leaves, and people in Kashmir wrote on birch bark. All paper is made in the same way: from thin plant threads pressed together into a sheet. Tear a piece of paper slowly, and you can see those threads at the edge.
how_we_found_out.who: Cai Lun, an official at the Chinese emperor's court, and archaeologists in China in the 1900s
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Paper was invented by Cai Lun in China in the year 105.
